q: Which conditions convert cyclohexanone into N-benzylcyclohexanamine?
c: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> and NaBH<sub>4</sub> mixed at the start, CH<sub>3</sub>OH
h: The C–N bond forms through an imine. Which hydride reduces an iminium ion but leaves the ketone alone?
w: Reductive amination: the ketone and benzylamine form an imine/iminium ion under mildly acidic conditions, and sodium cyanoborohydride reduces the iminium ion much faster than it reduces the ketone, so the imine is trapped as it forms: PhCH2NH2, NaBH3CN, pH ≈ 6.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> first gives cyclohexanol, and an alcohol does not react with an amine (OH<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group).
The imine forms, but aqueous acid hydrolyzes it straight back to cyclohexanone and benzylamine; nothing reduces the C=N.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone faster than the imine forms, so most of the ketone ends up as cyclohexanol.

q: Which sequence converts 1-bromobutane into pentan-1-amine?
c: 1. potassium phthalimide, DMF  2. H<sub>2</sub>NNH<sub>2</sub>, ethanol, heat
1. NaCN, DMSO  2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat  3. SOCl<sub>2</sub>  4. NH<sub>3</sub>  5. Br<sub>2</sub>, NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. Mg, ether  2. H<sub>2</sub>C=O  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. NH<sub>3</sub>, heat
h: Count carbons: the amine has one more carbon than the bromide, and the new carbon carries the nitrogen.
w: Pentan-1-amine has five carbons and the NH2 on the new carbon, so the extra carbon and the nitrogen should arrive together, as cyanide. SN2 with NaCN gives pentanenitrile, and LiAlH4 reduces C≡N to CH2NH2: 1. NaCN 2. LiAlH4 3. H2O.
x: The Gabriel synthesis makes a primary amine with the same carbon count as the halide, so this gives butan-1-amine.
This builds pentanamide, but the Hofmann rearrangement (Br<sub>2</sub>, NaOH) removes the carbonyl carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>, giving butan-1-amine.
The Grignard route gives pentan-1-ol, but NH<sub>3</sub> cannot displace OH (hydroxide is a poor leaving group), so no amine forms.

q: Which reagent carries out the conversion shown?
h: Only the nitro group changes. Which reducing agent is selective for ArNO<sub>2</sub> over a ketone?
w: Dissolving-metal reductions in acid (Sn, SnCl2 or Fe with HCl) reduce an aromatic nitro group to the anilinium ion and leave a ketone untouched; NaOH then frees the amine: SnCl2, HCl; then NaOH.
x: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone to a secondary alcohol and does not reduce the nitro group.
Clemmensen conditions reduce the ketone C=O to CH<sub>2</sub> (and the nitro group as well), giving 4-ethylaniline.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ketone, and with aromatic nitro groups it gives azo compounds rather than a clean aniline.

q: Which sequence converts butanoic acid into hexan-3-one?
h: You need to add exactly one ethyl group to the acyl carbon and stop at the ketone. Which organometallic reacts with acid chlorides but not with ketones?
w: Converting the acid to the acid chloride makes a strong acylating agent. A Gilman reagent transfers one alkyl group to an acid chloride but reacts only slowly with the ketone it forms, so the reaction stops at the ketone: CH3CH2CH2C(=O)CH2CH3, hexan-3-one.
x: Grignard reagents add to the ketone as fast as it forms, so two ethyls add and the product is 3-ethylhexan-3-ol.
The Grignard reagent simply deprotonates the carboxylic acid; the carboxylate salt does not accept a second Grignard addition, and workup returns butanoic acid.
This makes butanal and then adds ethyl, so the product is the alcohol hexan-3-ol, not the ketone.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Ozonolysis of cyclohexene opens the ring to a six-carbon dialdehyde. Which α-carbon can reach the other C=O to form a strain-free ring, and what does heat do to the aldol?
w: O3 then (CH3)2S cleaves cyclohexene to hexanedial, OHC(CH2)4CHO. In hot NaOH the enolate at C2 attacks C6, closing a five-membered ring (C2–C6); dehydration gives the conjugated cyclopent-1-ene-1-carbaldehyde. NaBH4 reduces the aldehyde (1,2) to the primary alcohol and leaves the C=C: (cyclopent-1-en-1-yl)methanol.
x: B forms only if the aldol product does not dehydrate and the ring C=C is never made; heating with NaOH drives the elimination to the conjugated enal first.
A six-membered ring would need a seven-carbon dialdehyde; hexanedial can only close a five-membered ring (or a strained three-membered one).
Dimethyl sulfide gives a reductive workup, so the ozonide gives the dialdehyde, not adipic acid; adipic acid would also not undergo aldol reactions.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohex-2-en-1-one into 2-(3-oxocyclohexyl)acetic acid?
c: 1. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C  2. CH<sub>2</sub>(CO<sub>2</sub>Et)<sub>2</sub>, NaOEt, EtOH  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
1. CH<sub>2</sub>(CO<sub>2</sub>Et)<sub>2</sub>, NaOEt, EtOH  2. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, 25 °C
h: The new CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H sits on C3, the β-carbon. Which nucleophile adds 1,4 and is a synthetic equivalent of <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H?
w: Diethyl malonate anion is a soft, stabilized nucleophile that adds 1,4 (Michael addition) to the β-carbon of the enone. Hot aqueous acid then hydrolyzes both esters and decarboxylates the malonic acid, leaving CH2CO2H on C3: 1. CH2(CO2Et)2, NaOEt 2. H3O+, heat.
x: LDA makes the enolate at C6 (α′), so the new CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H ends up on the α-carbon next to the C=O, not on C3.
After hydrogenation there is no C=C to accept a Michael addition, so the malonate cannot bond to C3.
Saponification at 25 °C gives the substituted malonic acid; without heat it does not lose CO<sub>2</sub>, so the product keeps two CO<sub>2</sub>H groups.

q: Which sequence converts toluene into 2-bromo-1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (separate the para isomer)  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH
h: In the target, Br is ortho to CH<sub>3</sub> and meta to NO<sub>2</sub>. In which intermediate do both groups send Br to that carbon?
w: Nitration of toluene gives 4-nitrotoluene (CH3 directs ortho/para). In 4-nitrotoluene, CH3 directs to C2 (ortho to itself) and NO2 directs meta to itself, which is also C2: the effects reinforce, and bromination gives 2-bromo-1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene.
x: In 4-bromotoluene the activating CH<sub>3</sub> controls nitration, which goes ortho to CH<sub>3</sub>; the product is 4-bromo-1-methyl-2-nitrobenzene (Br and NO<sub>2</sub> swapped).
Br<sub>2</sub> with light brominates the benzylic CH<sub>3</sub> by a radical pathway, giving 4-nitrobenzyl bromide.
The first two steps give the target, but Sn/HCl then reduces the nitro group to NH<sub>2</sub>, giving 3-bromo-4-methylaniline.

q: Which sequence converts benzene into 3-bromophenol?
c: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C  5. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C; then H<sub>2</sub>O, heat  4. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  2. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C  5. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 0 °C  5. H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>
h: OH and Br are both ortho/para directors, yet they are meta in the target. Which meta director can later be turned into OH?
w: Neither OH nor Br directs meta, so a meta director must place the Br and then be converted to OH. NO2 directs bromination meta; reduction gives 3-bromoaniline; diazotization and warming in water replace N2+ with OH: nitrate, brominate, reduce, NaNO2/H2SO4, H2O/heat.
x: Phenol is strongly activated and directs ortho/para; bromination gives 2- and 4-bromophenol (and polybromination), not the meta isomer.
Bromine directs nitration para (and ortho), so the sequence ends with 4-bromophenol.
H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> replaces the diazonium group with H, not OH, so the product is bromobenzene.

q: Which diene and dienophile give the Diels–Alder product shown as the major regioisomer?
h: The new ring C=C is between old diene C2 and C3. Where is the CH<sub>3</sub> relative to that C=C, and how far is it from the ester carbon?
w: In the product the ring C=C came from C2=C3 of the diene and the CO2CH3 sits on a carbon from the dienophile. The methyl is on a carbon of the ring C=C, so it was on C2 of the diene: isoprene. Isoprene and methyl acrylate give mainly the "para" (1,4) adduct, with CH3 and CO2CH3 on C4 and C1 of the cyclohexene: isoprene + methyl acrylate.
x: With methyl methacrylate both the CH<sub>3</sub> and the ester end up on the same sp<sup>3</sup> carbon (methyl 1-methylcyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate).
A 1-substituted diene gives the "ortho" (1,2) adduct, methyl 2-methylcyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate, with the CH<sub>3</sub> on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon next to the ester.
Both substituents come from the dienophile, so they end up on adjacent sp<sup>3</sup> carbons (methyl 6-methylcyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate).

q: Which sequence gives the racemic trans diol shown?
c: 1. buta-1,3-diene + diethyl fumarate, heat  2. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, ether; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. buta-1,3-diene + maleic anhydride, heat  2. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, ether; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. buta-1,3-diene + diethyl maleate, heat  2. LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, ether; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. buta-1,3-diene + diethyl fumarate, heat  2. NaBH<sub>4</sub>, ethanol
h: The Diels–Alder reaction is stereospecific: groups trans on the dienophile end up trans on the ring. Then ask which hydride reduces esters.
w: The Diels–Alder reaction keeps the dienophile geometry: a trans (E) dienophile gives trans substituents, a cis (Z) dienophile gives cis. Diethyl fumarate (E) gives racemic trans-diethyl cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylate, and LiAlH4 reduces both esters to CH2OH without touching the stereocenters: diethyl fumarate, then LiAlH4.
x: Maleic anhydride is a cis dienophile, so the adduct and the diol made from it are cis (the meso diastereomer).
Diethyl maleate is the Z isomer, so the two ester groups, and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH groups made from them, are cis.
The stereochemistry is right, but NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not reduce esters, so the diester is recovered.

q: Which sequence converts cyclohexene into racemic trans-2-methoxycyclohexan-1-ol?
c: 1. OsO<sub>4</sub>, NMO  2. NaH (1 equiv); then CH<sub>3</sub>I
1. mCPBA, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  2. NaOCH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OH  3. NaH; then CH<sub>3</sub>I
h: Trans-1,2 groups on a ring come from backside opening of a three-membered ring.
w: Epoxidation gives cyclohexene oxide; methoxide then opens it by SN2 from the face opposite the epoxide oxygen, so OCH3 and OH end up trans (anti opening). The product is racemic because attack at either carbon is equally likely: 1. mCPBA 2. NaOCH3, CH3OH.
x: OsO<sub>4</sub> adds both OH groups to the same face (syn), so methylating one of them gives the cis isomer (along with dimethylated product).
Alkoxymercuration–demercuration adds CH<sub>3</sub>O and H across the C=C, giving methoxycyclohexane with no OH.
The first two steps make the target, but NaH/CH<sub>3</sub>I then methylates the remaining OH, giving trans-1,2-dimethoxycyclohexane.

q: A student plans to make 4-ethylaniline from benzene as shown. Which step fails, and why?

s.arrow: 1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH

c: Step 3: the basic NH<sub>2</sub> group binds AlCl<sub>3</sub>, which strongly deactivates the ring toward Friedel–Crafts alkylation
Step 1: nitration of benzene needs FeBr<sub>3</sub> as the catalyst rather than H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to make NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
Step 2: Sn/HCl reduces the benzene ring to cyclohexane along with the nitro group
Step 3: the primary ethyl cation rearranges, so the product is 4-isopropylaniline, not 4-ethylaniline
h: Friedel–Crafts reactions need a Lewis acid. What does a Lewis acid do when it meets a Lewis base such as an amine?
w: Steps 1 and 2 give aniline normally. In step 3 the nitrogen lone pair binds AlCl3 (a Lewis acid–base complex), turning NH2 into a positively charged, strongly electron-withdrawing –NH2–AlCl3 group, so the ring does not undergo Friedel–Crafts alkylation. Step 3 fails. A workable route alkylates benzene first, nitrates (separating the para isomer), and then reduces.
x: Nitration uses H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to generate the nitronium ion; FeBr<sub>3</sub> is the bromination catalyst, and step 1 works.
Dissolving-metal reduction converts NO<sub>2</sub> to NH<sub>2</sub> and leaves the aromatic ring intact.
An ethyl group cannot rearrange to anything more stable (there is no isopropyl skeleton in two carbons); the problem is the Lewis acid–amine complex.

q: A student plans the route shown to 4-(hydroxymethyl)cyclohexan-1-one. Which step fails, and why?
c: Step 2: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is too weak to reduce an ester; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is needed
Step 1: ethylene glycol reacts with the ester rather than with the ketone
Step 3: aqueous acid cannot remove an acetal; TBAF is needed
Step 2: NaBH<sub>4</sub> attacks the acetal carbon and opens the ring
h: Check each reagent against the group it must change: acetal formation, ester reduction, acetal removal.
w: The plan is sound in outline: protect the ketone as an acetal, reduce the ester to CH2OH, and remove the acetal with aqueous acid. The flaw is the hydride: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones but not (at a useful rate) esters. With LiAlH4 in step 2 the route works. Step 2 fails.
x: Acetal formation is selective for the ketone; an ester carbonyl does not form an acetal under these conditions.
Acetals are hydrolyzed by aqueous acid; TBAF removes silyl ethers.
Acetals are stable to hydride reagents and bases, which is why they work as protecting groups during reductions.

q: What is the product of the sequence shown, starting from (R)-butan-2-ol?
h: Tosylation does not touch the stereocenter; one later step does. Then check what LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does to C≡N, and reassign R/S with the new groups.
w: TsCl/pyridine makes the tosylate with retention (the C–O bond is not broken). Cyanide displaces tosylate by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile (CN outranks ethyl and methyl, like OH did, so the inverted center is S). LiAlH4 reduces C≡N to CH2NH2 without touching the stereocenter; CH2NH2 still outranks ethyl, so the product is (S)-2-methylbutan-1-amine.
x: This is the R amine, which would require retention in the cyanide step; S<sub>N</sub>2 at the secondary tosylate inverts the center.
This is the nitrile from step 2; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> then reduces C≡N to CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, so the nitrile is not the final product.
This is the nitrile with retention; it is wrong at both the stereocenter (S<sub>N</sub>2 inverts) and the functional group (step 3 reduces it).

q: Which sequence converts 1-bromopropane into butanal?
c: 1. Mg, ether  2. H<sub>2</sub>C=O  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. Mg, ether  2. CO<sub>2</sub>  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. Mg, ether  2. ethylene oxide  3. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>  4. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
h: Butanal has four carbons. How many does each electrophile add, and which oxidant stops at the aldehyde?
w: Propylmagnesium bromide plus formaldehyde adds one carbon and gives butan-1-ol after workup. PCC (anhydrous) oxidizes a primary alcohol only to the aldehyde: 1. Mg 2. H2C=O 3. H3O+ 4. PCC.
x: Jones reagent is aqueous: the aldehyde forms a hydrate and is oxidized further to butanoic acid.
Carboxylation gives butanoic acid, which PCC cannot convert to an aldehyde (PCC is an oxidant, and the acid is already more oxidized).
Ethylene oxide adds two carbons, so the alcohol is pentan-1-ol and PCC gives pentanal.

q: Which reaction, followed by the workup shown, gives 1,1-diphenylpropan-1-ol?
h: An ester plus excess Grignard reagent gives a tertiary alcohol with two identical groups from the Grignard. Which two groups on the carbinol carbon are identical?
w: Esters react with two equivalents of a Grignard reagent (addition, loss of alkoxide to give a ketone, second addition), so the carbinol carbon carries two identical R groups from RMgX and the acyl group of the ester. The target carbinol carbon has two phenyls and one ethyl: the ethyl comes from the ester (propanoate) and both phenyls from PhMgBr: ethyl propanoate + excess PhMgBr.
x: Here the two identical groups are ethyls, giving 3-phenylpentan-3-ol.
A Gilman reagent adds once to an acid chloride and stops at the ketone, propiophenone; it does not add a second phenyl.
Ethyl benzoate supplies the third phenyl as well, giving triphenylmethanol.

q: Which sequence converts 2-methylcyclohexan-1-one into 2,6-dimethylcyclohexan-1-one (as a mixture of stereoisomers)?
h: The new methyl goes on the less substituted α-carbon. Which conditions form the less substituted enolate?
w: The new CH3 must go on C6, the less substituted α-carbon. LDA, a strong, bulky base at −78 °C, removes the more accessible C6 proton fastest and irreversibly (kinetic enolate); alkylation with CH3I then gives 2,6-dimethylcyclohexanone.
x: Under equilibrating conditions the more substituted (thermodynamic) enolate dominates, so methylation occurs at C2 and gives mainly 2,2-dimethylcyclohexanone.

Acid-catalyzed bromination goes through the more substituted enol, so Br goes on C2; any methyl introduced there ends up at C2, not C6 (and the cuprate does not cleanly substitute a tertiary bromide).
The Grignard reagent adds to the C=O, giving 1,2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol; the ketone is lost.

q: What is compound X, isolated after a neutral aqueous workup?
h: Step 1 protects one carbonyl. Which carbonyl forms an acetal, and what does LiAlH<sub>4</sub> do to the other one?
w: Ethylene glycol and acid convert the ketone (not the ester) of ethyl acetoacetate into a cyclic acetal. LiAlH4 then reduces the ester to a primary alcohol; the acetal, which is stable to hydride and base, survives a neutral workup. X is the acetal-protected 4-hydroxybutan-2-one; aqueous acid would later remove the acetal.
x: Butane-1,3-diol forms only if the ketone is unprotected; the acetal keeps the ketone carbon from being reduced.
4-Hydroxybutan-2-one is what forms after acid removes the acetal; the neutral workup leaves the acetal in place.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not stop at the aldehyde; the aldehyde formed after loss of ethoxide is reduced at once to the alcohol (DIBAL-H at −78 °C would be needed to stop at the aldehyde).

q: Which reaction is the best way to make ethyl 2-methyl-3-oxo-3-phenylpropanoate?
c: ethyl benzoate (excess) + ethyl propanoate, NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
ethyl benzoate + ethyl acetate, NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
ethyl propanoate alone, NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
benzaldehyde + ethyl propanoate, NaOEt, EtOH; then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
h: A β-keto ester comes from a Claisen condensation. Disconnect the bond between the ketone carbon and the α-carbon: which ester gives the acyl group and which gives the enolate?
w: Disconnecting the C2–C3 bond of the β-keto ester splits it into an acyl donor, PhC(=O)– from ethyl benzoate, and an ester enolate, −CH(CH3)CO2Et from ethyl propanoate. Ethyl benzoate has no α-H, so it can only be the electrophile, and using it in excess limits propanoate self-condensation: crossed Claisen of ethyl benzoate and ethyl propanoate.
x: Ethyl acetate supplies <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Et, so the product lacks the 2-methyl group (ethyl 3-oxo-3-phenylpropanoate).
Self-Claisen of ethyl propanoate puts a propanoyl group on the α-carbon, giving ethyl 2-methyl-3-oxopentanoate, with no phenyl.
An aldehyde acceptor gives an aldol-type β-hydroxy ester (or its dehydration product), not a β-keto ester.

q: Which sequence converts butane-1,3-diol into 4-hydroxybutan-2-one?
c: 1. TBSCl (1 equiv), imidazole, 0 °C  2. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  3. TBAF, THF
1. TBSCl (1 equiv), imidazole, 0 °C  2. TBAF, THF  3. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>
1. TBSCl (1 equiv), imidazole, 0 °C  2. PCC, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
h: Only the secondary alcohol is oxidized. Which OH does the bulky TBSCl silylate faster, and when must the TBS group come off?
w: The bulky TBSCl reacts selectively with the less hindered primary OH, protecting it as a TBS ether. PCC then oxidizes the free secondary alcohol to the ketone, and fluoride removes the silyl group to reveal the primary alcohol: 1. TBSCl (1 equiv) 2. PCC 3. TBAF.
x: Without protection PCC oxidizes both alcohols, giving 3-oxobutanal (the primary OH becomes an aldehyde).
Removing the TBS group before oxidation leaves both OH groups free again, so PCC oxidizes both.
Hydrogenation does not cleave a TBS ether, so the product is still the silyl-protected ketone.
